title: Flip-chip integrated superconducting qubits using electroplated bump bonds
authors: Yen-An Shih, Rebecca Gharibaan, Barka Khan, Dhananjay Joshi, Siddharth Singh, Martijn F. S. Zwanenburg, Eugene Y. Huang, Nataliia Zhurbina, Figen Yilmaz, Lukas Johannes Splitthoff, Srijit Goswami, Christian Kraglund Andersen
abstract: Flip-chip integration offers a promising route toward scalable superconducting quantum processors and hybrid semiconductor-superconductor quantum devices. We develop a three-dimensional transmon architecture using electroplated indium in which the qubit electric field is shared nearly equally between two bump-bonded substrates while maintaining low participation at the indium-bump interface. The resulting geometry is well suited for future hybrid qubits, enabling the integration of distinct material platforms while minimizing sensitivity to bump-interface loss. Using this platform, we evaluate electroplated indium interconnects for superconducting quantum circuits. Flip-chip transmons incorporating electroplated indium bumps exhibit qubit quality factors around $10^6$. In addition, a systematic study of coplanar-waveguide resonators is used to identify losses associated with the electroplating process. In particular, we find that surface losses associated with the gold-layer, used to enable good electric contact with the indium, is likely the primary contributor to the qubit decay rate. These results demonstrate the compatibility of electroplated indium technology with high-coherence superconducting circuits and establish a promising platform for three-dimensional hybrid quantum integration.
summary: This paper presents a method for building scalable superconducting quantum processors using flip-chip integration via electroplated indium bumps. By characterizing the qubit coherence and systematically analyzing loss sources across different fabrication steps, the authors demonstrate compatibility with high-coherence circuits while identifying surface losses at the gold interface as the main limitation.
main_problem: Developing a scalable, high-coherence platform for superconducting quantum processors by integrating distinct material platforms using flip-chip bonding.
main_result: The electroplated indium bump bond technology is compatible with high-coherence circuits, achieving qubit quality factors around $10^6$. The primary loss mechanism identified is surface loss associated with the gold layer used for electrical contact.
method: Fabrication and characterization of transmon qubits using a three-dimensional flip-chip architecture bonded via electroplated indium bumps. Loss mechanisms were systematically studied by comparing qubit lifetimes to resonator quality factors under controlled process variations.
model_or_system: The system is a 3D transmon circuit utilizing two substrates connected by electroplated indium bumps. The design aims to share the electric field across both substrates, minimizing sensitivity to interface losses.
key_observables: Qubit quality factor ($Q_i$), $T_1$ relaxation time, and resonator quality factors measured under varying magnetic fields and process steps.
important_parameters: Achieved $Q_i \approx 10^6$; dominant loss tangent ($	an \delta_{	ext{MA}}$) associated with the Au-covered metal-air interface.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that surface losses at the gold/metal-air interface are the primary limiting factor, and that field sharing across substrates is effective for coherence preservation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the flip-transmon cross-section, measurement distributions of internal quality factors over time, and plots comparing $Q_i$ vs. simulated energy participation ratios ($	ext{PAu,MA}$) to confirm loss sources.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the 3D transmon architecture using electroplated indium. It then systematically measures qubit coherence ($T_1$) and compares these results with resonator measurements across controlled process variations (e.g., presence/absence of Au film) to pinpoint the dominant loss mechanism, concluding that surface losses govern performance.
why_interesting: The work directly addresses scalability challenges in superconducting quantum computing by providing a robust, high-coherence integration technique compatible with advanced 3D packaging methods.
